title: Erdős #396 OQ-04 → OQ-01 → OQ-01 → OQ-02 → OQ-02 → OQ-01: The Central Binomial Coefficient as a Telescoping Wallis Product
description: The multiplicative twin of the parent's additive 1/2-exponent bound. Instead of taking logarithms of the central-binomial recurrence, this entry keeps the product: the recurrence (n+1)·C(2(n+1),n+1) = 2(2n+1)·C(2n,n) multiplies the sequence by s n = (4n+2)/(n+1) at every step, so it collapses to the finite product C(2n,n) = ∏_{k<n} s k. Normalising each factor by the limiting rate 4 turns this into the classical Wallis partial product in closed form: C(2n,n)/4^n = ∏_{k<n} (2k+1)/(2k+2) = (2n−1)!!/(2n)!!. Every Wallis factor lies strictly in (0,1), so the normalised sequence C(2n,n)/4^n is strictly decreasing; since it equals 1 at n = 0, the elementary bound C(2n,n) < 4^n (for n ≥ 1) drops out of the product alone — no (2n choose n) ≤ 2^{2n} is used. No Stirling estimate is used.

overview.historicalContext: The parent entry (Erdős #396 OQ-04 → OQ-01 → OQ-01 → OQ-02 → OQ-02) extracts the 1/2 critical exponent of the central binomial coefficient C(2n,n) from its two-term recurrence by the *additive* route: writing each normalised step s k / 4 = 1 − (1/2)/(k+1), the inequality log y ≤ y − 1 telescopes the logarithm of the recurrence to log(C(2n,n)/4^n) ≤ −(1/2)·H_n ∼ −(1/2)·log n. This file is the *multiplicative* twin — exactly the relationship that the Catalan telescoping product (Erdős #396 OQ-04 → OQ-01 → OQ-01 → OQ-01) bears to the Catalan 3/2-exponent file. Keeping the product rather than its logarithm exposes the classical Wallis partial product, the discrete object whose limit is Wallis' product for 2/π.
overview.problemStatement: Read multiplicatively rather than additively: does the central-binomial recurrence collapse to a finite product, and what is the closed form of the normalised sequence C(2n,n)/4^n?
overview.text: The recurrence (n+1)·C(2(n+1),n+1) = 2(2n+1)·C(2n,n) reads as multiplication by s n = (4n+2)/(n+1) at each step, so C(2n,n) = ∏_{k<n} s k (telescoping product). Dividing by 4^n = ∏_{k<n} 4 distributes factor-by-factor and gives C(2n,n)/4^n = ∏_{k<n} (2k+1)/(2k+2), the Wallis partial product (2n−1)!!/(2n)!!. Each factor (2k+1)/(2k+2) ∈ (0,1), so the normalised sequence is strictly decreasing; as it is 1 at n = 0, the bound C(2n,n) < 4^n for n ≥ 1 follows directly from the product.
overview.proofStrategy: The ratio statement C(2(n+1),n+1) = s n · C(2n,n) over ℝ is obtained by casting Mathlib's Nat.succ_mul_centralBinom_succ and clearing denominators (congrArg cast, push_cast, field_simp, linear_combination). A one-line induction with Finset.prod_range_succ telescopes it to C(2n,n) = ∏_{k<n} s k (centralBinom_eq_prod). Taking Real.log of the product recovers the parent's additive bridge log(C(2n,n)) = ∑_{k<n} log(s k) (log_centralBinom_eq_sum). The normalised factor s k / 4 is simplified to the Wallis term (2k+1)/(2k+2) (cbRatioQuarter_eq_wallis); each such term is strictly in (0,1) (wallisFactor_pos, wallisFactor_lt_one). Writing 4^n = ∏_{k<n} 4 (Finset.prod_const) and applying Finset.prod_div_distrib produces the Wallis product form C(2n,n)/4^n = ∏ (2k+1)/(2k+2) (centralBinom_div_eq_wallis_prod). Strict monotonicity (centralBinom_div_strictAnti) follows from strictAnti_nat_of_succ_lt: the multiplicative step is s n / 4 < 1 acting on a positive quantity. Finally, since the sequence equals 1 at n = 0 and strictly decreases, C(2n,n)/4^n < 1 for n ≥ 1, i.e. C(2n,n) < 4^n over ℝ and (by casting) over ℕ (centralBinom_lt_four_pow, centralBinom_lt_four_pow_nat).
keyInsights: **The recurrence is a telescoping product.** C(2n,n) = ∏_{k<n} (4k+2)/(k+1): each application of Mathlib's recurrence multiplies by one ratio, so the whole coefficient is a finite product of recurrence ratios — the multiplicative counterpart of the parent's additive log-sum.

**The normalised coefficient is the Wallis partial product.** C(2n,n)/4^n = ∏_{k<n} (2k+1)/(2k+2) = (2n−1)!!/(2n)!!. This is the truncation of Wallis' product for 2/π, exhibited here purely from the integer recurrence with no analytic input.

**Strict monotonicity is immediate from the product.** Every factor (2k+1)/(2k+2) lies strictly in (0,1), so multiplying by the next factor strictly decreases the (positive) normalised sequence; C(2n,n)/4^n is strictly decreasing in n.

**The 4^n bound falls out of monotonicity.** Because the normalised sequence starts at 1 (n = 0) and strictly decreases, C(2n,n)/4^n < 1 for every n ≥ 1, giving C(2n,n) < 4^n with no appeal to the row-sum bound (2n choose n) ≤ 2^{2n}.

**Strict decrease is not the same as the sharp rate.** This entry certifies only C(2n,n)/4^n < 1; the precise asymptotic decay C(2n,n)/4^n ~ 1/√(πn) — equivalently the infinite Wallis product ∏ (2k)²/((2k−1)(2k+1)) → π/2 — needs genuinely analytic input (e.g. Stirling or the Wallis integral) beyond any finite truncation of the same product. The elementary bound formalized here is exactly the boundary before that limit is taken.
prerequisites: Telescoping finite products (Finset.prod_range_succ) and the product/quotient lemmas Finset.prod_const, Finset.prod_div_distrib
Strict monotonicity of natural-indexed sequences (strictAnti_nat_of_succ_lt) and the logarithm of a finite product (Real.log_prod)

sections.title: Overview & Scope
sections.summary: Module docstring: the multiplicative twin of the parent's additive 1/2-exponent route. Keeping the product (not its log), the central-binomial recurrence collapses to a telescoping product whose normalisation is the Wallis partial product C(2n,n)/4^n = (2n−1)!!/(2n)!!, recovering C(2n,n) < 4^n with no row-sum estimate and no Stirling.

sections.title: The Recurrence Ratio and Telescoping Product
sections.summary: The ratio s n = (4n+2)/(n+1) read off Mathlib's recurrence; the normalised one-step lemma C(2(n+1),n+1) = s n · C(2n,n); the telescoping product C(2n,n) = ∏_{k<n} s k; and the log bridge log C(2n,n) = ∑_{k<n} log(s k) back to the parent's additive view.

sections.title: The Wallis Partial Product
sections.summary: The normalised factor s k/4 = (2k+1)/(2k+2) ∈ (0,1), and the headline identity C(2n,n)/4^n = ∏_{k<n} (2k+1)/(2k+2) = (2n−1)!!/(2n)!!, the truncation of Wallis' product for 2/π, distributed factor-by-factor from the telescoping product.

sections.title: Strict Decrease and the 4ⁿ Bound
sections.summary: The normalised sequence C(2n,n)/4^n is strictly decreasing (each step multiplies by the Wallis factor < 1), so starting from 1 it stays below 1 for n ≥ 1, giving C(2n,n) < 4^n purely from the product — no appeal to (2n choose n) ≤ 2^{2n}.

sections.title: Sanity Checks
sections.summary: Worked small cases: the empty product equals C(0,0)=1, the k=0 Wallis factor is 1/2, C(2,1)/4 = 1/2, the first strict drop, and C(4,2)=6 < 16.

conclusion.summary: The central-binomial recurrence collapses to the telescoping product C(2n,n) = ∏_{k<n} (4k+2)/(k+1), whose normalisation by 4^n is the Wallis partial product C(2n,n)/4^n = ∏_{k<n} (2k+1)/(2k+2) = (2n−1)!!/(2n)!!. Each Wallis factor lies strictly in (0,1), so the normalised sequence is strictly decreasing and, starting at 1, stays below 1 — recovering C(2n,n) < 4^n for n ≥ 1 from the product alone. All 13 theorems are fully machine-checked with no axioms or sorries.
conclusion.implications: Together with the parent's additive 1/2-exponent bound, this gives the two classical readings of the same recurrence: the logarithm telescopes to a harmonic sum (additive, exponent 1/2), while the product telescopes to the Wallis partial product (multiplicative, closed form). The Wallis form is the natural bridge to the analytic identity ∏_{k≥1} (2k)(2k)/((2k−1)(2k+1)) = π/2, and the strict-monotonicity / 4^n bound are obtained without any factorial asymptotics.
openQuestions: Does the Wallis partial product C(2n,n)/4^n = (2n−1)!!/(2n)!! converge to 0 with the rate √(1/(πn)) that the parent's harmonic bound predicts, i.e. can Mathlib's Wallis-product development be aligned with this exact double-factorial form to certify C(2n,n) ∼ 4^n/√(πn)?

Does the analogous telescoping product for the Catalan numbers (catalan n = ∏ r k) combine with this one through C(2n,n) = (n+1)·catalan n to give a single product identity in which the linear factor n+1 appears explicitly as the ratio of the two Wallis-type products?
